implementation_notes: Go's package initialization is already order-safe: the specification initializes package-level variables stepwise in dependency order, and Go 1.21 pinned the package ordering algorithm, so the static initialization order fiasco cannot arise for package state and no guard structure is needed. First-use construction of a shared value is done with sync.OnceValue (or sync.Once plus a variable) from the standard library, which runs the initializer exactly once and makes every caller wait for it; the fast path afterwards is an atomic load, so there is no reason to hand-roll a nil check with its missing happens-before edge.
pitfalls: sync.Once marks the call complete even if the function panics, so a panicking initializer leaves the value unset and later callers silently receive the zero value; sync.OnceValue and sync.OnceFunc (Go 1.21) cache the panic and re-panic instead, which is the safer default.

Package variables are initialized in a single goroutine before main, in dependency order and then by lexical file name - a specified order, but still an order no one should design around; init() has no error channel, so fallible setup belongs in an explicit function.
sync.Once protects construction only: the value handed out must be immutable or internally synchronized, otherwise the first-use guard gives false confidence.
There is no reset: tests that touch the accessor before their fixtures get production state, and lazily built package data leaks between test cases.
